1415.title: Asalha again
1415.hook: the first sermon, heard a fourth year
1415.howItsDone: On the Asalha full moon, Theravada Buddhists visit temples, listen to or chant the first sermon, the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, keep extra precepts, and often walk around the temple holding candles, flowers and incense.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Poson and a tracker following footprints, with one line: who brought it.

How does a sermon end? Usually, people stand up and go home. The first sermon ends differently. In the Deer Park near Benares, the Buddha finishes speaking to five ascetics, and the sutta turns its camera upward. The gods of the earth hear it and shout: the wheel has been set rolling, and nobody in the world can turn it back. The gods above them hear the shout and pass it on, heaven after heaven, all the way up. The whole world system trembles, and a great light appears. You've heard this sermon on Asalha's full moon before: the middle way, the four truths. This fourth time, listen for a quieter pattern inside it.
screen: `A SERMON IN THE DEER PARK.` → `THE SHOUT GOES UP.` → `A PATTERN INSIDE.`

segments.voice: First, the four truths, short. There is suffering. It has a cause, craving. It can end. And there's a path to its ending. Now the pattern. In the sutta, the Buddha doesn't just name each truth; he walks around each one three times. This is suffering; suffering is to be fully understood; it has been fully understood. This is the cause; it is to be let go; it has been let go. This is the ending; it is to be seen for yourself; it has been seen. This is the path; it is to be walked; it has been walked. Each truth gets a different job: understand, let go, see, walk. Suffering isn't something you abandon; it's something you understand. Craving isn't something you study forever; it's something you set down. Why did this matter? In the sutta, he says that until his knowing was clear in all these ways, he didn't claim to be fully awake. Only when he'd walked around every truth did he say it. Then the wheel. The sermon's title is the setting in motion of the wheel of the teaching. A wheel is something you push once, and then it rolls. In Theravada lands, the Asalha full moon keeps that first push in memory, and the next day the rains retreat traditionally begins. Each year the wheel is heard again, and each year someone hears it as if for the first time.
screen: `FOUR TRUTHS, SHORT.` · `EACH TRUTH, THREE TIMES.` · `UNDERSTAND, LET GO, SEE, WALK.` · then, large: `THE WHEEL TURNS.`

segments.voice: Say the sermon's outline silently, one line per breath: there is suffering, to be understood; there is a cause, to be let go; there is an ending, to be seen; there is a path, to be walked. Say it again, slower, and the third time let each line touch one small, real thing in your day: a sore back, a craving for your phone, a moment of quiet, a step you could take. Then let the words go and sit with the breath.
Asalha. The full moon that remembers the first sermon in the Deer Park, when the wheel of the teaching was set rolling. Today's word.
Your line: the wheel turns. One push, and it keeps on rolling. See you on the next turn.

1416.title: The rains retreat again
1416.howItsDone: In Theravada countries monks enter the rains retreat after the Asalha full moon, each declaring a dwelling for the season; some lay people take on extra precepts or give something up for the same months.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first sermon heard again, each truth with its own job, and the line: the wheel turns.

A monk has just promised to stay put for the whole rainy season. Then a message comes. A lay family who supports the monastery wants him to come and bless a new house, a few days' walk away. Or worse: his mother is ill. Does he go? Does the promise mean staying inside the monastery walls no matter what? The monks in the Buddha's time asked exactly this kind of question, and the answers are in the monastic rule. You've met the rains retreat before, and how it began with complaints about trampled crops. Today, look at the promise itself: what it holds, and where it bends.
screen: `A PROMISE TO STAY PUT.` → `THEN A MESSAGE COMES.` → `WHERE DOES IT BEND?`

segments.voice: First, the promise. At the start of the rains, each monk settles into one dwelling and declares that he will spend the rains retreat there. In Pali the season is vassa, the rains. It isn't a vow of silence or a lockdown. It's a vow of place. Then the bend. The monastic rule, in the section on entering the rains, allows a monk to leave on short business, up to seven days, and return. When? If he's sent for by a lay supporter who wants to give a gift or hear the teaching. If a fellow monk or nun is sick and needs help. If his mother or father is ill. The rule is careful: he goes, does what's needed, and comes back inside the time. So the retreat isn't a wall against people. It's a home base you return to. Why staying matters: wandering is good for meeting people; staying is good for going deep. In one place for a season, the same path to the same well, the same room, the same faces, there's less to plan and more room to practice. By custom, a monk's seniority is even counted in rains. Last, the lay side. In Theravada lands, some lay people take on a practice for the season too: keeping extra precepts on moon days, giving something up, or going to the temple more often. Not a season in a monastery; just one thing, kept in one place, all season long.
screen: `A VOW OF PLACE.` · `LEAVE FOR NEED, THEN RETURN.` · `STAYING LETS IT GO DEEP.` · then, large: `STAY IN ONE PLACE.`

segments.voice: Feel where you're sitting, the floor, the chair, the room around you: a place you could return to. Bring back the one practice you chose a few days ago and ask: could I keep this one thing for the season, here, not perfectly, just coming back the way a monk comes back inside the seven days? If it feels too big, make it smaller until it fits, and rest in the place itself.
The rains retreat. Vassa, the season when monks stay in one place, leaving only briefly for real need. Today's word.
Your line: stay in one place. A vow of place still bends for someone who needs you. Rain or shine, see you tomorrow.

1417.title: Ullambana
1417.hook: the Chinese festival of offering for ancestors, from Moggallana's mother
1417.howItsDone: In Chinese and other East Asian Buddhist communities, families bring offerings to temples in the seventh lunar month and register the names of deceased ancestors and living relatives, while monks chant the Ullambana assembly.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rains retreat: a vow of place that bends for real need. Your line: stay in one place.

Paper slips cover a long wall in a Chinese temple hall, row after row, each with a name brushed onto it. Some names belong to the dead: a grandfather, a mother, a baby who didn't live long. Some belong to the living: a sick father, a child taking exams. In front of the wall, tables are heaped with fruit, rice, flowers and cloth. Monks file in and chant. This is the Ullambana assembly, held in the seventh lunar month. You've met its Japanese cousin, Obon, with its fires and dances. Today, stay in the Chinese hall, and ask why the wall holds the names of the living as well as the dead.
screen: `NAMES ON PAPER SLIPS.` → `THE DEAD AND THE LIVING.` → `WHY BOTH?`

segments.voice: First, the story, told a few days ago at the home altar. In the Ullambana Sutra, a Chinese Buddhist scripture, the disciple Moggallana finds his dead mother among the hungry ghosts and can't feed her himself. The Buddha sends him to give, on the day the monks finish their summer retreat, to the whole community of monks: food, bowls, bedding, the things they need. Then what the sutra does next, which is easy to miss. It doesn't stop with one mother. Moggallana asks whether other disciples, in times to come, could make the same offering for their own parents. The Buddha says yes, and widens it. Then the living. The sutra says the same offering helps parents who are still alive, bringing them long life and freedom from illness, and it reaches back through the generations of ancestors too. That's why the paper slips carry both kinds of names. Last, what the festival became. The sutra ends with the Buddha telling disciples who care for their parents to make this offering every year, on the fifteenth day of the seventh month. In China and across East Asia, families still bring names and offerings to temples in that month. Some readers hear in it a festival about care that runs both ways in time: for the parents who are still here, and the ones who came before them.
screen: `HE CAN'T FEED HER HIMSELF.` · `GIVE TO THE WHOLE COMMUNITY.` · `FOR THE LIVING AND THE DEAD.` · then, large: `FOR THE ANCESTORS.`

segments.voice: Let one parent or ancestor come to mind, living or gone, or, if no one in your family feels right, a teacher or someone who raised you; picture their face, or just their name. Think of one small thing you could offer to others in their name, groceries for a food bank, a meal for a neighbor, an hour of help, and rest with them as you breathe. If someone's absence weighs too much to hold alone, you can call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.
Ullambana. The festival of offering for ancestors and living parents, from the story of Moggallana's mother. Today's word.
Your line: for the ancestors. A name brushed on paper can hold a whole family. That's today, done.

1418.title: Pavarana again
1418.hook: invite honest feedback at the end of the rains
1418.howItsDone: At the end of the rains retreat, Theravada monks gather on the full moon for Pavarana, and each in turn invites the community to point out any fault seen, heard or suspected; lay people often bring offerings to the temple that day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ullambana: a gift for one mother, widened to every parent. Your line: for the ancestors.

"Be honest. Tear it apart." A friend hands you a draft, a business plan, a wedding speech. So you're honest. You point out the slow middle and the joke that doesn't land, and you watch their face close like a door. They asked for it, and they didn't want it. Asking is the easy part. Hearing is hard. At the end of the rains retreat, monks gather for a ceremony called Pavarana, the invitation, and each one asks the others to name his faults. You've met it before. This time, look at the second half: what the one who asks promises to do with the answer.
screen: `BE HONEST. TEAR IT APART.` → `ASKING IS EASY.` → `HEARING IS HARD.`

segments.voice: First, the words. In the monastic rule, each monk, in turn, invites the community: if you've seen anything, or heard anything, or even suspected anything, speak to me out of compassion, and seeing it, I will make amends. Notice the three doors he opens: seen, heard, suspected. He's not only asking about what's been proven. He's letting people bring a worry. Second, why they may speak: out of compassion. Not to win, not to score a point after a season together. The invitation sets the tone for the answer. Third, the promise at the end. Seeing it, I will make amends. That's the part the friend with the wedding speech forgot. The one who asks isn't just bracing to be hurt; he's agreeing ahead of time to look, and to fix what he finds. Fourth, why it's needed. The Dhammapada says, in Max Müller's words: "The fault of others is easily perceived, but that of oneself is difficult to perceive." The verse is plain about blind spots. Another verse goes further, and calls the person who points out your faults someone who shows you where treasure is. In paraphrase: if you find a wise person who reproves you, stay close to them, the way you'd follow someone who knows where gold is buried. It will be better for you, not worse. So Pavarana isn't a punishment at the end of the rains. It's a community lending each other their eyes.
screen: `SEEN, HEARD, SUSPECTED.` · `SPEAK OUT OF COMPASSION.` · `SEEING IT, I WILL MAKE AMENDS.` · then, large: `TELL ME MY FAULTS.`

segments.voice: Think of one person who knows you well and wishes you well, and picture asking them, gently: is there one thing I do that's hard to be around? Notice what happens in your body, a lifted shoulder, a tight jaw; then picture hearing their answer, whatever it is, and saying back: thank you, I'll look at that. Rest there, with the door open, and let the breath stay slow.
Pavarana. The invitation at the end of the rains, when each monk asks the others to name his faults, and promises to make amends. Today's word.
Your line: tell me my faults. Asking takes one breath; hearing takes two. Until tomorrow.

1419.title: Kathina again
1419.howItsDone: In Theravada countries, in the month after the rains retreat, lay people bring robe cloth and other useful gifts to a monastery in a Kathina ceremony, and the community gives the cloth to one monk to make into a robe.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pavarana: seen, heard, suspected, and a promise to make amends. Your line: tell me my faults.

A heavy rain is falling on the city of Savatthi. A servant girl runs to the monastery with a message: the meal is ready, the monks are invited. She comes back puzzled. There are no monks there, she says, only naked ascetics standing out in the rain. Her mistress, a wealthy laywoman named Visakha, understands at once. The monks had taken off their robes to bathe in the rain, because they had no other cloth to bathe in. They're monks, she tells the girl. Go back. The rains retreat ends in gifts, and Kathina is its robe offering. You've met it before. Today, meet the woman in the monastic rule who taught the community what a useful gift looks like.
screen: `RAIN ON SAVATTHI.` → `NO MONKS, ONLY ASCETICS?` → `THEY HAD NOTHING TO BATHE IN.`

segments.voice: After the meal, the rule says, Visakha asks the Buddha for a favor. He answers that awakened ones don't grant favors blindly. So she names what she wants: to give, for as long as she lives, cloth for monks to bathe in during the rains. Food for monks arriving in town who don't know where to go for alms. Food for monks setting out on a journey. Food and medicine for the sick, and food for the ones nursing them. Rice gruel in the mornings. And bathing cloth for the nuns. Then the Buddha asks her why. What good does she see in each one? She answers each, plainly. The new arrival, tired and lost, can eat and then go looking. The nurse doesn't have to leave the sick monk to fetch food. Every item comes from paying attention to someone's real need. The Buddha grants her request and praises her giving. Now the line to Kathina. At the end of the rains, after months in one place, robes are worn thin. Lay people bring new cloth, and the community gives it to one monk to make a robe that day. It's a gift that fits the moment, just as Visakha's did. The Dhammapada says, in Max Müller's words, "let him overcome the greedy by liberality." Visakha's way of being liberal wasn't a grand gesture. It was noticing who was standing in the rain.
screen: `VISAKHA ASKS TO GIVE.` · `WHY EACH GIFT? SHE KNOWS.` · `NOTICE THE REAL NEED.` · then, large: `THE RAINS END IN GIFTS.`

segments.voice: Look around your own circle the way Visakha did: who is standing in the rain in some small way, a coworker new to town, a neighbor caring for a sick parent, a student far from home? Let one person come to mind and ask her question: not what would look generous, but what would actually help, a meal, a lift, an umbrella, literally. Choose one, then rest with the breath.
Kathina. The robe offering at the end of the rains, when lay people bring cloth and the community makes a robe for one monk. Today's word.
Your line: the rains end in gifts. The useful gift is the one that fits the need. See you after the rain.

1420.title: Lhabab Duchen again
1420.howItsDone: On Lhabab Duchen, Tibetan Buddhists visit temples, make offerings, recite prayers and mantras, circle stupas and holy places, and give generously; in Theravada lands the descent is remembered with alms rounds at the end of the rains.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kathina, and Visakha noticing monks standing in the rain. Your line: the rains end in gifts.

What do you owe the person who gave birth to you? People answer with flowers, phone calls, money, or a seat at the head of the table. The Buddha's own story has a strange shape here. Tradition says his mother, Maya, died soon after his birth, so he never had the chance to repay her in the ordinary ways. After his awakening, the story goes, he went up to the heaven where she had been reborn, and spent a rains retreat teaching her. Then he came down. In Tibet, the day of that descent is Lhabab Duchen. You've met the staircase of the gods before. Today, ask why he went up at all.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU OWE YOUR MOTHER?` → `HE NEVER KNEW HER.` → `WHY DID HE GO UP?`

segments.voice: A debt that can't be paid. In the Numbered Discourses, the Buddha says there are two people you can never fully repay: your mother and your father. Even if you carried one on each shoulder for a long life, washed and fed them, and made them rulers of the earth, it wouldn't be enough. They brought you up, fed you, and showed you this world. Then the discourse turns to the one way it can be repaid. If your parents lack faith, you help them toward faith. If they lack virtue, toward virtue. If they're stingy, toward generosity. If they lack wisdom, toward wisdom. That, it says, repays them. Read Lhabab Duchen beside that discourse, and the trip to heaven looks like a son repaying a debt. He didn't bring his mother gold. He brought her the best thing he had, the teaching. Last, the coming down. When the season ended, he didn't stay. Tradition says he descended at Sankassa, to crowds waiting below. In Tibet, Lhabab Duchen is kept with offerings, circling holy places, and giving. Elsewhere, at the end of the rains, the same descent is remembered with alms rounds. He went up to honor one person and came back down for everyone. Some readers see in that the whole shape of the path: go deep for someone you love, then return to the ordinary crowd.
screen: `A DEBT YOU CAN'T REPAY.` · `UNLESS YOU HELP THEM GROW.` · `HE BROUGHT HER THE TEACHING.` · then, large: `HE CAME DOWN.`

segments.voice: Let your mother come to mind, or whoever mothered you, a grandmother, an aunt, a father who did both jobs, a foster parent, a teacher; if that relationship is painful, choose someone else who cared for you, or simply rest with the breath. Breathe in and remember one thing they made, carried or fixed for you; breathe out and let a little thanks go toward them, living or gone. If missing someone feels heavy today, call or text 988 in the US, or local emergency help.
Lhabab Duchen. The Tibetan holy day of the Buddha's descent from heaven, after teaching his mother. Today's word.
Your line: he came down. Underneath the festival, a son and his mother. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1421.title: Rohatsu again
1421.hook: the week of sitting for the awakening
1421.howItsDone: In Zen monasteries in Japan and elsewhere, monks and lay practitioners sit an intensive week-long retreat called Rohatsu sesshin, ending on the day kept for the Buddha's awakening, sometimes sitting through the final night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lhabab Duchen: a debt to a mother, repaid with the teaching. Your line: he came down.

The last night of the week. In a cold Zen hall, nobody has lain down. The candles are low. Legs ache. Someone's stomach growls, loud, and nobody laughs. Then the windows begin to gray, and low in the east, before the sun, one bright point of light hangs over the trees. In Zen tellings, that's the moment: the seeker under the tree looks up at the morning star and wakes. Rohatsu is the week of sitting that ends there. You've stayed through the last night before, and the middle of the week with Mara's army. This year, listen for what tradition says came out of his mouth when it was over.
screen: `THE LAST NIGHT OF THE WEEK.` → `ONE BRIGHT POINT IN THE EAST.` → `WHAT DID HE SAY?`

segments.voice: First, the verses. The Dhammapada holds two short verses that the commentary tradition places on the Buddha's lips at the moment of awakening. He speaks to a builder: the one who keeps putting up the house of a self, life after life. He says he went looking for that builder through many births, and birth again and again was painful. Then the turn, in Max Müller's words: "But now, maker of the tabernacle, thou hast been seen; thou shalt not make up this tabernacle again." Tabernacle is an old word for a tent or a house. The verse goes on to say the rafters are broken and the ridge-pole shattered. Who is the builder? The commentary reads it as the mind's own craving, the thirst that keeps reaching and keeps making a shelter out of me and mine. It was never an enemy outside. It was a habit, and once it was seen clearly, it couldn't keep building. So why a week of sitting? The house isn't taken down by force. It's seen. And seeing needs stillness, so for a week, from before dawn into the night, people in Zen halls sit and watch the builder at work: the plans, the worries, the little stories of who they are. This week on the path walked the festival year: the wheel set rolling, the rains, the ancestors, the invitation, the gifts, the descent. It ends where the teaching began: one person, sitting still until the morning star.
screen: `TWO VERSES AT THE AWAKENING.` · `THE BUILDER HAS BEEN SEEN.` · `CRAVING BUILDS THE HOUSE.` · then, large: `THE MORNING STAR.`

segments.voice: Sit as still as is comfortable and watch for the builder: a plan for later, a worry about someone, a story about yourself. Don't fight it; just notice, there's the builder picking up a plank, and come back to the breath, again and again. When the bell rings, stay a little longer if you can, the way the Zen halls sit through the night; even one more breath counts.
Rohatsu. The Zen week of sitting that ends on the day kept for the awakening, when tradition says the Buddha saw the morning star. Today's word.
Your line: the morning star. One bright point before sunrise, and a builder seen. A week of festivals, done.
